CEST-detectable metabolite candidates: liver

3 of 5 candidates clear the simulated with-vs-without contrast threshold (0.5%) at some field strength, by chemical exchange (downfield, +ppm) or by the relayed NOE (upfield, −ppm). 0 fall below it; 2 are unknown because no group had a verified reference rate, so nothing could be simulated. The threshold applies to our own simulation, never to a literature MTRasym.

  • Glycogen: ✓ detectable (rNOE)
  • Glutamine: ✓ detectable (chemical exchange)
  • Glutathione: ✓ detectable (chemical exchange)
  • Glutamate: ? unknown (not simulated)
  • Alanine: ? unknown (not simulated)

Excluded before simulation (not stored in the tissue): [model's own exclusion] Taurine (no explicit >1 mM parenchymal concentration quote found in retrieved abstracts); [model's own exclusion] Histidine (no explicit >1 mM parenchymal concentration quote found in retrieved abstracts); [model's own exclusion] Mobile Protein Pool / APT (CEST signal confirmed, but no explicit mM concentration value found in retrieved literature); [model's own exclusion] Glycosaminoglycans (not physiologically significant in liver parenchyma); [model's own exclusion] Bicarbonate (present in bile/secretions, not stored in parenchymal cells); [model's own exclusion] Lipid CH2 (not an exchangeable proton pool for CEST); [model's own exclusion] Choline-containing compounds (mostly quaternary amines, no exchangeable protons)

Recommended field strength(s): 3 T, 5 T, 7 T

Robustness to input uncertainty: robust

Uncertainty corners: Contrast over the uncertainty corners (Hydroxyl (-OH) [hydroxyl]: concentration 24-53 mM, kex fixed at 31850 s−1 (single measurement, spread unknown); Aliphatic C-H (rNOE) [rnoe]: concentration 24-53 mM, kex fixed at 5 s−1 (single measurement, spread unknown)) at the swept B1/Tsat: 0.5 T: 0.10-0.23%, 1.5 T: 0.23-0.51%, 3 T: 0.39-0.85%, 5 T: 0.57-1.25%, 7 T: 0.64-1.41%. Threshold 0.5%. Detectable even at the low corner.

Frequency-collision analysis: At 1.5 T and above, the rNOE peak (-1.1 ppm) is within the broad linewidth of the semisolid MT pool (-2.4 ppm). The simulation shows separation <166 Hz at 3T vs MT linewidth ~16 kHz. They blur. rNOE cannot be resolved as a distinct peak from MT in liver. At 0.5 T, hydroxyl (+1.0) is far from MT but merges with fast-exchanging amine/Thiol signals if they were simulated.

Direct water saturation: At 0.5 T, direct saturation bandwidth (10.6 Hz) is small compared to the 1.0 ppm offset (500 Hz). No masking. At higher fields, the Hz gap increases, so direct saturation remains negligible for the rNOE peak.

Ex vivo / in vivo exchange-rate caveat: rNOE rate (5 s−1) is borrowed from protein phantoms (PMID 25996515). In vivo liver crowding may alter relay rates. Hydroxyl kex is from mouse phantom (PMID 38933551). Liver pH/crowding differs.

Optimized saturation sequence by field strength (derived from a Bloch-McConnell B1×Tsat sweep):

  • 0.5 T: B1=0.25 µT, Tsat=500 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) —
    recommended sequence: 0.167% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 1.5 T: B1=0.25 µT, Tsat=2000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) —
    recommended sequence: 0.365% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 3 T: B1=0.25 µT, Tsat=3000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) — Slow-exchanging rNOE pool ($k_{ex}=5 s^{-1}$). Low B1 maximizes contrast without saturating water or collapsing MT. Long Tsat compensates for slow transfer.
    recommended sequence: 0.615% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 5 T: B1=0.25 µT, Tsat=3000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) — Same physics as 3T. Higher field increases Hz separation from MT, improving resolvability slightly, but low B1 is still optimal for slow exchange rNOE.
    recommended sequence: 0.903% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 7 T: B1=0.25 µT, Tsat=3000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) — Max contrast at 7T. Low B1 preserves MT baseline. High field maximizes Hz separation between rNOE (-1.1) and MT (-2.4).
    recommended sequence: 1.019% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied

B1/Tsat vs. extraction method (click for note + literature)

Note: Low B1 (0.25 µT) is required to avoid collapsing the MT pool which overlaps the rNOE signal. AREX or multi-pool Lorentzian fitting is necessary to distinguish rNOE from MT. MTRasym is unreliable due to asymmetric MT background.

No citations.

Potential clinical impact

glycoCEST (glucosyl protons, ~1 ppm): 2 CEST/NOE application and 2 metabolite-change studies verified (2 human, 2 animal; 0 humans, 0 animals; 6 dropped by verification). CEST evidence for glycogen (glycoCEST) exists in metabolic (fasting/refeeding) and inflammatory (CCl4 injury) contexts in human and rat liver. Metabolite-change evidence supports glycogen depletion in ALD, MAFLD/MASLD, and post-exercise states across species. Clinical applicability strongest for metabolic liver disorders and acute injury models.

Caveats / critique (7 points, 349 words) — Concentration 38.1 mM is plausible for glycogen-loaded liver. However, the simulation uses small-solute T1/T2 (1.0s/10ms) for a large macromolecular aggregate. …
  • Concentration 38.1 mM is plausible for glycogen-loaded liver. However, the simulation uses small-solute T1/T2 (1.0s/10ms) for a large macromolecular aggregate. Glycogen granules have much shorter T2, which would broaden the pool and reduce effective CEST contrast compared to the simulated sharp-pool approximation. Hydroxyl protons at +1.0 ppm are fast-exchanging ($k_{ex} > 30,000 s^{-1}$).
  • They do not form a distinct CEST peak but rather broaden water directly. The rNOE pool at -1.1 ppm is the primary source of detectable contrast. The agent correctly separates these, but the hydroxyl 'CEST' signal is negligible. rNOE peaks from glycogen are well-documented in muscle, but liver rNOE is confounded by protein MT.
  • rNOE shift for glycogen is typically reported around -1.0 to -1.2 ppm in muscle. Liver environment may shift this slightly due to crowding, but -1.1 ppm is a reasonable estimate. None significant for CEST. The hydroxyls are simulated. Amine/Amide are absent.
  • verifying_citations: PMID 36161668 (claimed as 'MR multitasking for robust quantification of tissue characteristics and metabolic imaging in the human liver') dropped PubMed's actual title is 'Free-breathing 3D CEST MRI of human liver at 3.0\xa0T.'. verifying_citations: PMID 39529314 (claimed as 'In vivo detection of glycogen in mouse skeletal muscle using chemical exchange saturation transfer (CEST) MRI') dropped
  • PubMed's actual title is 'Simultaneous monitoring of glycogen, creatine, and phosphocreatine in type II glycogen storage disease using saturation transfer MRI.'. verifying_citations: PMID 25996515 (claimed as 'Relayed nuclear Overhauser enhancement in chemical exchange saturation transfer (CEST) MRI: simulation and experimental verification') dropped
  • PubMed's actual title is 'Transfer Rate Edited experiment for the selective detection of Chemical Exchange via Saturation Transfer (TRE-CEST).'. extraction_method_citations: PMID 25542802 (claimed as 'Quantitative chemical exchange saturation transfer (CEST) MRI using the exponential fitting model (AREX)') dropped PubMed's actual title is 'Label-free imaging of gelatin-containing hydrogel scaffolds.'.
  • no SAR or hardware ceiling is applied: the recommended B1/Tsat is the sweep optimum, and deliverability must be checked against the scanner's SAR monitor Exchangeable protons are the hydroxyl groups on the glucosyl repeat unit (3 per internal unit). CEST signal detected at ~1.0 ppm.

Recommended field strength(s): 7 T

Robustness to input uncertainty: fragile

Uncertainty corners: Contrast over the uncertainty corners (Amide (Side Chain) [amide]: concentration 7-20 mM, kex 15-158 s−1) at the swept B1/Tsat: 0.5 T: 0.03-0.26%, 1.5 T: 0.07-0.76%, 3 T: 0.10-1.45%, 5 T: 0.14-2.04%, 7 T: 0.15-2.26%. Threshold 0.5%. Only the point estimate clears the threshold; the low corner does not.

Frequency-collision analysis: Glutamine Amide (+3.5 ppm) and Glutathione Amide (+3.5 ppm) have 0 Hz separation. They are physically indistinguishable in the simulation. They will appear as a single peak. Glutamate has no amide, so it does not collide here. The 'Glutamine CEST' signal is actually 'Glutamine + Glutathione Amide CEST'.

Direct water saturation: Peak at 3.5 ppm is far from water. Direct saturation bandwidth (up to 32 Hz at 7T) does not overlap.

Ex vivo / in vivo exchange-rate caveat: Amide kex (65.5 s−1) is borrowed from brain/in vivo liver medians. Actual liver kex depends on local pH. The spread (15-158 s−1) reflects this uncertainty.

Optimized saturation sequence by field strength (derived from a Bloch-McConnell B1×Tsat sweep):

  • 0.5 T: B1=0.5 µT, Tsat=750 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) —
    recommended sequence: 0.075% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 1.5 T: B1=0.5 µT, Tsat=3000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) —
    recommended sequence: 0.224% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 3 T: B1=0.75 µT, Tsat=3000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) —
    recommended sequence: 0.338% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 5 T: B1=0.75 µT, Tsat=3000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) — Amide kex ~65 s−1 is intermediate. Higher B1 (0.75 µT) improves saturation transfer efficiency compared to low B1. Long Tsat ensures full saturation.
    recommended sequence: 0.476% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied
  • 7 T: B1=0.75 µT, Tsat=3000 ms, continuous wave (CW-equivalent B1,rms from simulation sweep) — Same regime. Higher field allows slightly higher B1 without excessive direct saturation, but 0.75 is optimal for kex ~65.
    recommended sequence: 0.530% contrast; no SAR ceiling applied

B1/Tsat vs. extraction method (click for note + literature)

Note: MTRasym is invalid due to asymmetric MT background and overlap with Glutathione. Multi-pool Lorentzian fitting is required to deconvolve MT from Amide. AREX is preferred for quantification.

No citations.

Potential clinical impact

amine protons (potentially ~2-3 ppm, but not established for liver): 0 CEST/NOE application and 2 metabolite-change studies verified (2 human, 0 animal; 59 humans, 0 animals; 3 dropped by verification). No CEST application studies for glutamine in liver were found. Metabolite-change evidence shows glutamine increases in brain during hepatic encephalopathy and decreases in arterial blood during tumor-bearing states. Liver-specific glutamine changes are implied (liver switches from glutamine balance to output in cancer). CEST application in liver remains unexplored.

  • Concentration 7.0 mM is within range, but uncertainty [7-20] mM seems high for fasting liver; 20 mM is more typical of tumors. The simulated contrast scales linearly with concentration, so higher concentrations in pathology could increase signal. Correctly identifies two amide groups. Simulates them as a single pool at 3.5 ppm. This is standard for amide CEST.
  • The amine group is correctly excluded as not simulated. Amide shift at 3.5 ppm is standard. In vivo pH variations can shift this by +/- 0.1 ppm. Amine protons are fast-exchanging and not simulated. They contribute to background/broadening but not distinct CEST.

Glutathione — CEST: ✓ detectable (chemical exchange)

Concentration: 9.50 mM typical (7-10 mM) animal evidence only

Estimated concentration — no direct literature value found. Reasoning: The study reports hepatic tissue GSH levels of 9.50 ± 0.55 μmol/g wet weight in untreated rats. Assuming liver tissue density is approximately 1 g/mL (standard for aqueous tissue), 1 μmol/g wet weight converts directly to 1 mM. Thus, 9.5 μmol/g ≈ 9.5 mM. This represents the total reduced glutathione pool in the hepatocyte cytosol.

Glutamate — CEST: ? unknown (not simulated)

Concentration: 5.00 mM typical (2-8 mM) animal evidence only

Estimated concentration — no direct literature value found. Reasoning: Glutamate and glutamine levels are tightly coupled via glutamine synthetase. In healthy liver, glutamine is typically higher than glutamate. Reference data for liver amino acid pools (e.g., from Williamson & Brosnan in Bergmeyer's Methods of Enzymatic Analysis) places glutamate in the low mM range (2-10 mM). PMID 41094143 confirms high periportal glutamate in mouse liver. PMID 30360490 confirms glutamate is a major amino acid in key metabolic organs. A typical value of ~5 mM is a conservative estimate for healthy parenchymal tissue.

In vivo verification: ROI-differential CEST scan — axial, centered at T11 vertebral level to encompass the right hepatic lobe and spleen.

Why this scan: Comparing liver (high metabolite) vs spleen (low metabolite) in the same axial slice controls for B0/B1 inhomogeneity and generic MT/NOE background. If contrast at specific offsets tracks concentration differences (Liver > Spleen), it confirms metabolite-specific CEST.

ROIWhere it is drawnRole
liver target tissueRight lobe central parenchyma, avoiding major vessels and capsule.Target tissue with high concentration of all candidate metabolites.
spleenCentral splenic parenchyma.Comparison tissue with significantly lower glycogen and glutathione levels.

Scan protocol: 3 T, pulsed Gaussian train, B1=0.5 µT, 32 pulses × 25 ms (interpulse delay 25 ms, duty cycle 50%), total Tsat=1600 ms, TR=3000 ms

SAR reasoning (the experimentalist agent's own; the pipeline applies no SAR model): 50% duty cycle at 0.5 µT yields low specific absorption rate. 1600 ms total saturation is well within abdominal SAR limits at 3T.

Compromise rationale: B1=0.5 µT favors Glutathione (optimal ~0.5-0.75 µT) and matches Glycamine's amine exchange. It slightly under-saturates Glutamine (optimal ~0.75 µT) but preserves SAR budget and signal-to-noise ratio better than higher B1.

Fat suppression: SPIR (Spectral Attenuated Inversion Recovery) prepulse to suppress signal from hepatic lipid and visceral fat, preventing spectral overlap and baseline distortion.

Motion mitigation: Respiratory navigator gating or split breath-holds (15s per Z-spectrum segment) to minimize motion artifacts in the liver/spleen region during saturation train.

Slice coverage: Axial slab, 10 mm thickness, centered at the T11/T12 disc space to ensure inclusion of both liver right lobe and spleen parenchyma.

Structures in FOV: liver, spleen, kidney, spinal cord

Z-spectrum sampling offsets:

  • -5.00 ppm: baseline
  • -3.50 ppm: rNOE reference
  • -1.00 ppm: Glycogen aliphatic C-H (rNOE)
  • +0.00 ppm: water (0 ppm)
  • +2.20 ppm: Glutamine alpha-NH3+
  • +2.50 ppm: Glutathione thiol/amine
  • +7.20 ppm: Glutathione/Glutamine amide
  • +8.00 ppm: baseline

  • sweep_b1_grid_uT: [0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0, 4.0, 5.0, 6.0]
  • sweep_tsat_grid_ms: [500, 750, 1000, 1500, 2000, 3000]
  • sweep_saturation_model: continuous wave, single shot from thermal equilibrium (CW-equivalent B1,rms)
  • b1_ceiling: no SAR or hardware ceiling is applied: the recommended B1/Tsat is the sweep optimum, and deliverability must be checked against the scanner's SAR monitor
  • tsat_choice: grid Tsat with the highest contrast at the best B1 (no scan-time shortening)
  • pool_t1_s: 1.0
  • pool_t2_s: 0.01
  • max_background_metabolites: 3
  • verification_scan_field_T: 3.0
  • verification_scan_model: the experimentalist's pulse train (rectangular pulses at its B1), 90 degree single-shot readout, exact periodic steady state at its TR, Z normalized to the same cycle without saturation
  • b1_inhomogeneity_fraction: 0.3
  • uncertainty_corners: contrast re-simulated at the swept B1/Tsat at every corner of [concentration range from the literature agent] x [kex spread of the reference tier]
  • llm_sampling: each model's served defaults; the pipeline sends no temperature or top_p

A FAILED completeness check means the agent's structured output never covered everything it was asked to (e.g. a verdict for every metabolite) within its retry budget, and the incomplete output was kept; the deterministic checks above flag what is missing.
